title: Soft Commodity Infrastructure (Brazil)
description:
Where Brazilian farms connect to markets. This is the geolocated midstream of
Brazilian agriculture: the silos, slaughterhouses, dairy plants, and sugar/ethanol
mills that farms sell into, plus the cooperatives that farms belong to. It exists
to answer, for any rural property, **who to contact** about deforestation on the
land - the cooperative that has the farmer as a member, or the buyer that receives
their grain, cattle, or cane.

## How it was made

Every point comes from a government registry, or is geocoded from one. Nothing is
guessed from satellite imagery.

- **Grain silos** - CONAB's national warehouse registry (`ArmazensCadastrados`),
  which every grain warehouse must register with. It ships real GPS coordinates,
  so these are exact. Includes cooperative, trader/private, and official silos.
- **Slaughterhouses & dairy plants, federal** - MAPA's SIF (federal meat/dairy
  inspection) registry. Has the company, tax ID, and address but no coordinates,
  so we geocoded the addresses ourselves. Beef, poultry, pork, dairy.
- **Slaughterhouses & dairy plants, state/municipal** - the smaller local plants
  (SIE/SIM/CONSORCIO) that a frontier producer often delivers to, which the
  federal list misses. These live in MAPA's SISBI system, which has no bulk
  download; Trase pulled the SISBI records and geocoded them from the registry
  addresses, and we use that subset. Registry-derived, not AI-detected.
- **Sugar/ethanol mills** - ANP's ethanol producer list (company, tax ID, town,
  capacity). No street address, so each mill sits at its town's center.
- **Cooperative membership** - IBGE's Censo Agropecuario 2017, which counts how
  many farms in each municipio belong to a cooperative. A density signal, not a
  named cooperative - but it works even in remote frontier towns.
- **Municipality geometry** - IBGE's official municipio boundaries.

## Trust labels on every row

Because not every point is equally precise, each carries two labels. **`basis`**
is `observed` (someone official recorded it) or `modelled` (we calculated it -
only the gravity-catchment rows). **`geom_method`** records how the coordinate
was set. Five values occur in the data: `registered` (18,796 rows, the source
gave the GPS coordinate), `geocoded` (12,007, an address turned into a point,
which can be off), `municipality` (5,257, the municipality polygon itself),
`derived` (3,103, modelled catchment areas) and `municipality_centroid` (1,506,
all that was available was the town). A user can see at a glance how good each
location is.

## Full methodology & source

Pipeline, tests, and a plain-language writeup live at
https://github.com/wri/rural-land (see `soft_commodity_infrastructure/METHODOLOGY.md`).
Brazil only. Rice, cotton, and coffee are not covered - no authoritative open
geolocated source exists for them.
